title: The Perfect Score
full_review:
Six high school students conspire to steal the answers to their college entrance exams in the below-the-bell-curve teen comedy "The Perfect Score" (Paramount).

While its attractive cast may click with some young viewers, the film's box-office score should be anything but perfect. And though Americans will continue to debate the effectiveness of standardized testing, the ineffectiveness of Brian Robbins as a director -- as evidenced by this film -- is less in question. If this movie were a test score, Robbins would be lucky to get into any form of higher education.

The framing of the story is simple. Six high school seniors devise an elaborate scheme to beat what they see as an unfair system -- a system they argue arbitrarily places greater emphasis on gender and racially biased test results than on a student's overall academic history -- by breaking into the Princeton Testing Center and swiping a copy of the answer key to the upcoming SAT test (which in this flick's case stands for Silly And Trite).

Masterminding the operation is Kyle (Chris Evans), a studious architect wannabe, who refuses to see his dreams of attending Cornell go down in the flames of his less-than-stellar 1020 SAT score, and his best friend Matty (Bryan Greenberg), who just wants to get accepted by the University of Maryland to be with his girlfriend. Using John's Hughes' "The Breakfast Club" (1985) as a creative crib sheet, Robbins surrounds Kyle and Matty with a motley crew of co-conspirators, each on board for different personal reasons.

Standing in for Molly Ringwald's pouty princess is valedictorian runner-up Anna (Erika Christensen), who, though capable of acing the test, wants to stick it to her Ivy League-obsessed parents. Ally Sheedy's antisocial outcast is updated as Francesca (Scarlett Johansson), a rebel with all the right belle curves whose cradle-robbing father owns the building they need to break into. Rounding out the club is an Emilio Estevez-like jock, Desmond (played by NBA star Darius Miles), a hoops phenom who needs to score high on the SAT to play college ball, and a Judd Nelson-esque slacker, stoner Roy (Leonardo Nam), who is just along for the ride.

As in any heist film, an inordinate amount of screen time is spent on the execution of their appointed mission. But, as is usually the case, their best-laid plans are sent awry by unforeseen obstacles, leading to unintended adolescent epiphanies -- usually of the "hey-you're-kinda-cute-by-flashlight" variety.

The film's below-average showing on the verbal portion of the test (cheesy dialogue and a stale, derivative plot) should be a portent of equally dismal results on the math section -- as in box office receipts. Much of what passes for dialogue is downright -- albeit unintentionally -- hilarious. As Desmond's mom puts it, "There's a whole lotta dumb dribbling out of your mouth."

The movie fosters the very stereotypes it purports to subvert, characterizing Desmond as an African-American whose only hope of a college degree depends on his excelling on the hardwoods, and Roy, an Asian-American, as a computer wiz.

More disconcerting, however, is the story's anti-authority undercurrent, which not so subtly imparts a kids-know-better-than-parents message, illustrated by Anna's rebellious metamorphosis from "good girl" to "bad girl." Giving the thumbs-up to the transformed Anna's new makeover, Francesca says, "You look like a slut. I like it."

In fairness, not all parental figures are demonized. Desmond's mom is portrayed as being sincerely concerned for her son's future, but her just-say-no-to-drugs public service announcements are so laughably forced that they severely dim the otherwise positive light in which she is cast. Also, the film sends mixed signals to young viewers concerning marijuana by condemning its use while at the same time containing scenes that incorporate it as opportunity for laughter.

And though the film's honesty-is-the-best policy ending should earn it at least a passing grade, the characters' virtuous reversal has less to do with any clear distinctions of "right" and "wrong" or recognition of the inherent immorality of cheating than it does with a vague sense of self-empowerment and feel-good fuzzies.

To paraphrase Roy's perceptive analogy: X is to Y as this film is to boring. Perhaps a more apt title would be "The Perfect Snore."
Due to an instance of rough language, as well as crude language, sexual humor and innuendo and several drug references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
